Two Stage Bounded Risk Point Estimation of a Normal Mean

Source: R/ts_br_norm_mean.R
ts_br_norm_mean.Rd

Evaluates the two stage bounded risk point estimation procedure for the mean \(\mu\) of a normal distribution whose variance is unknown. The loss in estimating \(\mu\) by the sample mean is \(A\,|\bar{X} - \mu|^k\) (absolute error for \(k = 1\), squared error for \(k = 2\)), and the goal is a sample size at which the expected loss, the risk, is at most w. The first stage (pilot_data) fixes the total sample size; the second stage (additional_data) completes it. The estimate is the mean of all observations from both stages. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

ts_br_norm_mean(pilot_data, additional_data = NULL, A, k, w, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

pilot_data

Numeric vector of the first stage observations, at least \(k + 2\). The whole first stage must be supplied at every call, because it alone determines the total sample size.

additional_data

Numeric vector of the second stage observations collected so far, or NULL (the default) when none have been collected.

A

The loss constant: the loss is \(A\,|\bar{X} - \mu|^k\). A single positive number, in the units of w per unit of error to the power k.

k

The error index: 1 for absolute error loss, 2 for squared error loss.

w

The risk bound: the largest acceptable expected loss. A single positive number.

na.rm

Logical. If TRUE (the default), missing values are removed from both stages before anything is computed; if FALSE, a missing value is an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with columns term and value and four rows:

mean

The mean of all observations supplied, the estimate of \(\mu\).

risk

The estimated risk of that mean at the current sample size, \(B\,(S^2 / n)^{k/2}\), with \(S^2\) the sample variance of all observations supplied. A descriptive estimate; the guarantee is the one stated in Details.

optimal_n

The total sample size \(N\) fixed by the first stage.

current_n

The number of observations supplied, both stages together.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), loss_A, k, risk_bound, method, and notes (always empty for this function). There is no conf_level or width, and no variance_unusable attribute: a first stage whose variance cannot be estimated is an error (see Details).

Details

If the standard deviation \(\sigma\) were known, the risk of the mean of \(n\) observations would be \(B\,(\sigma^2 / n)^{k/2}\) with \(B = A\,2^{k/2}\,\Gamma((k + 1)/2)/\sqrt{\pi}\) (which is \(A\) for \(k = 2\) and \(A\sqrt{2/\pi}\) for \(k = 1\)), and the smallest sample size meeting the bound would be \(n^* = (B / w)^{2/k} \sigma^2\). With \(m\) first stage observations and their sample variance \(S_m^2\), the total sample size is $$N = \max\{m,\ \lceil (b_m B / w)^{2/k} \, S_m^2 \rceil\}, \qquad b_m = \left(\frac{m - 1}{2}\right)^{k/2} \frac{\Gamma((m - k - 1)/2)}{\Gamma((m - 1)/2)}.$$ If \(N = m\) the first stage is enough; otherwise \(N - m\) further observations are collected, once. \(N\) depends on the first stage alone. The row optimal_n is this total \(N\), not the number still to collect.

The constant \(b_m\) is the expectation of \((S_m^2 / \sigma^2)^{-k/2}\), which exists only when \(m \ge k + 2\); for \(k = 2\) it is \((m - 1)/(m - 3)\). A smaller first stage is an error.

The guarantee is exact. For normal data the risk of the final mean is at most w for every \(\mu\), every \(\sigma\), and every first stage size \(m \ge k + 2\): \(N\) depends only on \(S_m^2\), which is independent of the sample means, so the risk is \(B \sigma^k E[N^{-k/2}]\), and \(N \ge (b_m B / w)^{2/k} S_m^2\) bounds that by w. The price is sample size: the expected \(N\) is about \(b_m^{2/k}\) times \(n^*\) (for \(k = 2\), \((m - 1)/(m - 3)\)), which is why ts_br_norm_mean_pilot does not return a very small first stage. The guarantee rests on normality.

A first stage with no variation is an error. If every first stage observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, the rule used throughout the package), the first stage variance cannot be estimated and the function stops with an error that says what to do. The purely sequential functions report such data as a stopping rule that is not yet met, with the attribute variance_unusable; here that would mislead, because the total sample size is fixed by the first stage alone, so no later observation could turn a rule reported as not met into one that is met. Data whose real variation is that small beside their size (times recorded in seconds since 1970 that differ by hundredths of a second, for example) should have a common value subtracted from both stages first; the total sample size does not depend on it.

Data on a scale so large or so small that a variance cannot be represented in double precision (observations beyond about \(10^{154}\), or differing by less than about \(10^{-154}\)) are an error that says to express them in other units; no row of the result is ever infinite.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

ts_br_norm_mean_pilot for the first stage size; seq_br_norm_mean for the purely sequential procedure.

Other ts_br_norm_mean: ts_br_norm_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# A clinic manager wants the mean waiting time (minutes) estimated with
# a mean squared error of at most 4, that is, squared error loss with
# A = 1 and risk bound w = 4.
set.seed(113)
m <- ts_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 2, w = 4)
first_stage <- rnorm(m, mean = 45, sd = 12)
check <- ts_br_norm_mean(first_stage, A = 1, k = 2, w = 4)
check
#> Sequential check (two stage bounded risk estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 43
#> 
#>   mean              : 41.24481
#>   risk              : 13.11412
#>   optimal_n         : 43
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The first stage fixed the total sample size; collect the remainder.
n_more <- attr(check, "criterion_n") - attr(check, "current_n")
second_stage <- rnorm(n_more, mean = 45, sd = 12)
ts_br_norm_mean(first_stage, second_stage, A = 1, k = 2, w = 4)
#> Sequential check (two stage bounded risk estimation (normal mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 43
#>   Criterion n     : 43
#> 
#>   mean              : 47.41062
#>   risk              : 3.74368
#>   optimal_n         : 43
#>   current_n         : 43
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
